episode_title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life)

stories.summary: The first column of Amit's 'Range Rover' poker column for the Economic Times imagined a young man whose favourite author is Milan Kundera. He walks into a bookshop and sees a pretty girl in a distant aisle reading Kundera. Should he go up and introduce himself? Even if he is diffident and puts the odds of a date at 10% and of finding a soulmate at 1%, those outcomes are worth so much that the approach is massively plus EV. A 90% rejection rate costs him only a moment of embarrassment.
stories.insight: Expected-value thinking is not only for gamblers. When the downside is tiny and the upside is huge, you should take the shot every time. Most of us already sense this intuitively, and naming it helps fear stop disguising itself as prudence.
stories.quote: it actually costs you nothing because it's a moment of perhaps embarrassment, but that's it. There's no cost to it.

stories.topic: Just Bet on the Side Batting Second
stories.summary: Before the 2016 IPL, a friend who dabbled in cricket betting asked Amit, by then retired from poker, for a tip. Amit's advice was to bet on the side batting second in every match. The friend expected deep nuance, ignored him, and called back after the 14th match. The chasing side had won 13 of the 14, comfortably, losing about 3.4 wickets on average and finishing in around 17 overs. Chasing gives a small informational edge worth perhaps 55-45 or 60-40, nothing like that. The real cause was that teams batting first kept underestimating the par score. Virat Kohli, captaining Bangalore, lost at least three games batting first and implied his bowlers were to blame because 'we got the par score'.
stories.insight: When the rules of a game change, people keep playing by the old mental model, and that creates a big, systematic edge for anyone who has updated. (Amit adds that cricket betting is illegal in India and he doesn't advise it.)
stories.quote: Why was there this massive skew? Because teams were underestimating the par score.

stories.topic: Amla and de Villiers Refuse to Score
stories.summary: On 6 December 2015, the fourth day of a Delhi Test, South Africa came out needing about 431 runs to win in a day and a half against India. They judged that a win was impossible on that pitch against those bowlers. Hashim Amla made 25 off roughly 244 balls, and AB de Villiers, one of the most aggressive batsmen ever, made 43 off about 293. People couldn't believe natural stroke-players were batting like this.
stories.insight: Aggressive cricket and aggressive batting are not the same thing. The same EV logic that demands attack in T20 demands total defence when there is no reward for risk. Doing the correct thing can look stupid to an audience judging by style.
stories.quote: Over here, there is no cost to a dot ball, and the value of a wicket is infinite.

stories.topic: From Gavaskar's 36 Not Out to Bazball
stories.summary: When ODIs arrived, teams played them like Test cricket. In the 1975 World Cup, Sunil Gavaskar batted all 60 overs for 36 not out, defending himself with 'I didn't play every ball'. The ODI game updated slowly. New Zealand sent Mark Greatbatch out as an early pinch-hitter, and in the 1996 World Cup Jayasuriya and Kaluwitharana attacked from the start, but the middle overs stayed a period of consolidation. About seven or eight years ago England front-loaded their ODI batting, made 300-plus scores routine outside the subcontinent, and won the 2019 World Cup, with some luck in the final. Under Brendan McCullum ('Baz') they then took this into Tests. Amit's ex-Cricinfo colleague Andrew Miller coined the term 'Bazball', which McCullum dislikes because 'it's not just all crash and burn'.
stories.insight: An entire sport can play a format suboptimally for decades because everyone inherits the previous format's habits. England's edge was not raw aggression. They were finally getting expected value right by looking at the data.
stories.quote: they were the first to recognize that the ODI game for the last three decades had actually been played wrong.

stories.topic: Johnny von Neumann vs the Coin Toss
stories.summary: At the time of the great debates between Einstein and others about probability in physics, John von Neumann asked whether a coin toss is truly random or merely Newtonian mechanics we haven't bothered to compute. He worked out formulas and heuristics that, given some initial facts about the coin, predicted the outcome at roughly 0.66 to 0.33. More recently, Ajay recalls, a project associated with Persi Diaconis had researchers around the world toss physical coins millions of times. They found that a coin starting heads-up lands heads about 51% of the time.
stories.insight: Much of what we call randomness is really our inability to compute. Even the textbook 50-50 event carries a tiny exploitable edge, and Ajay jokes that you can use it whenever you want to cheat at an important life decision.
stories.quote: is the randomness of a coin toss something truly random about the world, or it is our failure to compute?

stories.summary: Football is broken down to a science. When Amit wrote 'What Cricket Can Learn From Poker', Messi had a 12.1% chance of scoring when shooting from outside the box and 8% from a direct free kick. Coaches drill these numbers into players, so they know the EV of shooting versus passing to a striker. The data-driven 'playing out from the back' approach, from the Cruyff school and adopted by Pep Guardiola, led Guardiola on arriving at Manchester City to get rid of a goalkeeper good enough to play for England, because he couldn't play out from the back.
stories.insight: A tactic can look ridiculous in the moment, like a misplaced pass that gifts the opponent the ball, and still be right on average. Elite teams value players for what is plus EV, not for traditional skills done beautifully.
stories.quote: this whole logic of play out from the back can look ridiculous, you know, when you end up giving the ball away with a bad pass. And that sometimes happens. But on the whole it is plus EV.

stories.topic: Steel or Software? The Bet Everyone Makes Leaving College
stories.summary: When Ajay was leaving college, he would put a question to people his age. If you bought shares in a few industries and held them for 30 years, betting on whether steel or software would do well, everyone would call it speculative. Yet choosing an industry or a company is exactly that bet, made with your human capital. In the 1980s nobody could have known Indian pharma or Indian software would boom. Those who happened to choose them look brilliant, and the media then lionises them as geniuses.
stories.insight: People who think they are too risk-averse to touch the stock market are already making a concentrated, undiversifiable bet with their most important asset. Much celebrated success is luck that we retell as genius.
stories.quote: you're trading with your biggest undiversifiable asset, which is your own human capital, when you choose a workplace, when you choose an industry.

recommendations.item: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
recommendations.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation at the end of the episode.
recommendations.reason: A masterful primer on thinking probabilistically. It covered so much that Amit dropped his own plan to write a book on what poker taught him about probability. It shows why TV experts, who are incentivised to exude certainty, are often wrong, and teaches the humility to keep updating your priors and examining your biases.

recommendations.item: Thinking Strategically: The Competitive Edge in Business, Politics, and Everyday Life
recommendations.creator: Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode.
recommendations.reason: Draws on game theory ('strategically' in the sense of John von Neumann) and brings that body of knowledge close to real-world applications. Ajay thinks anyone grappling with reality will benefit from it.

recommendations.item: A First Course in Probability
recommendations.creator: Sheldon Ross
recommendations.context: Ajay names it as the probability 'wing' of his brain and asks Amit to connect it with cricket.
recommendations.reason: The classic probability textbook behind the episode's expected-value reasoning, for anyone who wants the rigorous maths beneath the intuitions.

recommendations.item: What Cricket Can Learn From Poker
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2016 Cricket Monthly piece, cited in the episode and listed as essential reading.
recommendations.reason: Amit's foundational case for applying expected value to cricket. It includes the football data example (Messi's 12.1% from outside the box versus 8% from free kicks) showing how far other sports had moved towards data.

recommendations.item: What Cricket Can Learn From Economics
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Essential reading in the show notes, the companion to the episode's opportunity-cost argument.
recommendations.reason: Applies the economist's idea of opportunity cost to cricket. This is the lens behind the episode's claim that T20's scarcity of deliveries makes dot balls costlier and wickets cheaper.

recommendations.item: Resources vs Constraints - Why T20 Teams Need to Attack More
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Essential reading in the show notes (2019).
recommendations.reason: Sets out the core T20 argument of the episode: the same 11 resources spread over only 20 overs means teams should attack far more than they do.

recommendations.item: The lesson from this IPL: Front-load your innings
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The 2014 ESPNcricinfo piece where, Amit says, he coined the term 'frontloading'.
recommendations.reason: The original argument that T20 teams should drop the pinch-consolidate-slog grammar inherited from ODIs and attack all the way through, sending hitters in first.

recommendations.item: Unlikely is Inevitable
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions the column while explaining why ten tails in a row needn't mean a weighted coin.
recommendations.reason: Explains the law of truly large numbers: given a big enough sample, any unlikely event is bound to happen, so streaks are not evidence of a bad decision.

recommendations.item: We Are All Gamblers
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit cites this 2010 column while arguing that traders aren't uniquely gambling.
recommendations.reason: Every action involves probabilities, from real estate versus other investments to software versus television as a career. We are all implicitly making probabilistic judgments, so 'gambler' shouldn't be an insult.

recommendations.item: The Bookshop Romeo
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The first column in Amit's Range Rover poker column, retold in the episode.
recommendations.reason: The Milan Kundera bookshop example: a high-reward, near-zero-cost approach is massively plus EV. It is a portable illustration of expected value in everyday life.

recommendations.item: Range Rover (archive of Amit's poker column)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions the poker column he wrote for the Economic Times for about a year.
recommendations.reason: The full set of columns in which he applied poker's probabilistic thinking beyond the poker table.

recommendations.item: Luck is All Around
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Listed in the show notes alongside the episode's discussion of luck.
recommendations.reason: Expands the episode's life lesson: luck plays a far bigger role than we realise, so don't let good luck make you arrogant or bad luck make you defeatist.

recommendations.item: Fair coins tend to land on the same side they started
recommendations.creator: František Bartoš et al.
recommendations.context: The show-notes source for Ajay's point about the global coin-tossing study.
recommendations.reason: The empirical basis for the finding that a coin tossed heads-up lands heads about 51% of the time, showing structure hidden inside apparent randomness.

recommendations.item: eventstudies (open-source R package)
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Ajay, a co-author, pitches it after proposing a research idea on whether a six changes what happens next.
recommendations.reason: An event study could measure whether a six shifts expected runs or wicket probability over the next few balls. Ajay invites anyone who wants to write that paper to talk to him.

core_ideas.concept: Expected Value: Judge the Decision, Not the Outcome
core_ideas.explanation: Take a bet that pays 51 paise on heads and costs 49 on tails: its EV is +1 paisa a flip, so you should take it. Yet you'll lose half the single flips, and even over a hundred flips you can still end up behind. Observers will call the right decision a blunder because of the result. Poker players are trained not to be results-oriented. Ajay calls judging policy by outcome a widespread analytical flaw, because many good decisions go wrong through dumb luck.
core_ideas.quote: I always like to say, don't judge a policy by an outcome.

core_ideas.explanation: Imagine every coin flip splitting the world into parallel universes: H or T, then HH, HT, TH, TT, and so on. Which universe you land in is pure luck. Given enough trials, even a hundred heads in a row will occur somewhere, which is the law of truly large numbers. So you can't evaluate your actions by how they worked out. Live by a good set of rules and don't sweat results.
core_ideas.quote: after something has happened, it has hundred percent happened or zero percent happened. But before anything happens, it is probabilistic.

core_ideas.concept: Luck Is Bigger Than We Think (Against the Great Man Theory)
core_ideas.explanation: Play Nadal at tennis or Magnus Carlsen at chess a hundred times and you lose every game. The best poker player against a beginner is closer to 51-49 per hand, because skill needs a long sample to show. Life works similarly. Lucky breaks such as where you were born can make you arrogant, and bad luck can make you defeatist, so sweat only what you control. Ajay adds that this runs opposite to the great man theory: celebrated CEOs often just happened to be in the right industry at the right time.
core_ideas.quote: luck plays a far greater role in our lives than we realise.

core_ideas.explanation: In polite Indian company, wise grown-ups supposedly don't speculate. Ajay argues that everything significant involves judgment under uncertainty: a surgeon choosing a diagnostic path, a financier allocating money, two people deciding whether to launch a new YouTube show. Only the most controlled, predictable work is free of speculation.
core_ideas.quote: So actually, if you wish to banish speculation from your life, then you probably want a very dull life.

core_ideas.concept: Above the API vs Below the API
core_ideas.explanation: An API call takes an instruction and reliably returns a predictable answer every time. The Uber driver lives below the API: code tells him to take this customer from here to there, and he has no agency. The people who design and decide, embracing risk, complexity and probabilistic thinking, live above it. Most interesting things happen above the API, and it is where one should aim to be.
core_ideas.quote: There are the people in the world who live above the API, and there are the people who live below the API.

core_ideas.concept: T20 Opportunity Cost: Scarce Balls, Cheap Wickets
core_ideas.explanation: ODIs give you 11 resources across 50 overs; T20 gives the same 11 resources across only 20. Deliveries become scarcer, so each dot ball costs more, each wicket is worth less, and the EV of aggression rises. Teams nonetheless carried over the ODI grammar of pinch-hitting, consolidating and slogging. Amit's prescription is to front-load: attack throughout and send hitters first, keeping 'builders' for when wickets fall. Finishing an innings with only two or three wickets down signals you weren't aggressive enough. As Ajay put it, 'You left money on the table.'
core_ideas.quote: the cost of a dot ball, a ball of which no run is scored, is much higher, and the value of a wicket is lower.

core_ideas.concept: Strike Rate Minus Required Strike Rate
core_ideas.explanation: In T20, averages and aggregates no longer matter; strike rate does. Amit's proposed metric is a batsman's strike rate minus the strike rate his team needed to reach the par score. If it's negative, he made the rest of the team carry his slowness, and the more runs he scores the bigger the liability. During a match the calculation shifts ball by ball. For example, losing three wickets in the first over raises the value of the remaining wickets and makes caution more valuable.
core_ideas.quote: if that number is negative, then the more runs he makes, the greater the liability he is to his team.

core_ideas.concept: Fix the Metrics, Fix the Incentives
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls this the quintessential problem of all organisations: personal objectives (looking good) diverge from team objectives (winning). Judge batsmen on averages and you push them towards suboptimal play. They should instead be judged against a hurdle rate, the rate needed to win. The fix must go upstream to selectors, just as hiring a star trader in a dumb way is management's fault. Amit adds the Indian history behind this. In eras when India usually lost abroad, Gavaskar-style chasing of personal landmarks made sense and stuck around. Selectors also find it safer to pick the guy with a good average than one who correctly risks his wicket and gets unlucky.
core_ideas.quote: it is possible to recruit a star trader in a dumb way, and it is the fault of the management that hired those star traders.

core_ideas.explanation: Experts on TV and Twitter are incentivised to exude certainty, but a complex world allows only probabilistic answers such as 70% this, 20% that. Forecasters who gave Trump a low chance in 2016 weren't necessarily wrong just because he won. Ajay says the conversation between economists and the real world is dysfunctional: people want a super-forecaster, and an honest economist must often say 'I don't know.' Better to talk about the forces at work than play the forecasting game.
core_ideas.quote: understanding finance is learning to respect the uncertainty of that beast.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's improvised intro paints Amit as a 'serious philosopher' who spends his nights reading complex books by German philosophers. Amit: 'I did, I confess, read German philosophers, but that is not something that one admits in public.' The show notes title the chapter 'What? He Reads German Philosophers? Scoundrel!'
Amit specifies a perfectly fair coin, 'not like the Sholay coin, but a proper legit coin', a nod to the famous coin in the film Sholay.
Amit promises to bring Asimov and Clarke into a probability lesson, explaining expected value through science-fictional parallel universes that split with every coin flip.
Ajay on von Neumann: 'Johnny to all his good friends. There's only one Johnny in the world, and that's Johnny von Neumann.'

Ajay's practical takeaway from the 51% coin-toss finding: 'whenever you want to cheat at important life decisions, offer to the blokes around you, let's toss the coin, and I've given you a slight edge.'

After Ajay's lecture on living above the API, Amit asks: 'I might get kicked out from your circle of friends for asking this question, but I have to. On behalf of our gentle listeners as well. What the fuck is an API?'

Amit's three possible outcomes of a skied shot: a six, a catch, or 'the ball hits a bird in the sky and then drops down on a fielder's head and the bird and the fielder die', which he calls 'incredibly unlikely, but nevertheless a non-zero possibility.'
Ajay: 'now shut up and give us cricket.' Amit: 'I can't shut up and give you cricket, I have to talk.'

Ajay recalls watching Sunil Gavaskar bat at Wankhede as a child and says Sachin Tendulkar grew up about fifty metres from him in Bandra East. Amit: 'A day should come when Sachin Tendulkar says, You know, I grew up in the same neighborhood as Ajay Shah. I would like that day to come.'

'Bazball', coined by Andrew Miller, Amit's ex-colleague at Cricinfo, after England coach Brendan 'Baz' McCullum. McCullum hates the label: 'I don't really like that silly term... It's not just all crash and burn.'

Harry Truman's plea for 'a one-handed economist', made because his advisers kept saying 'on one hand this, on the other hand that.' Amit sympathises with both Truman, who had to decide, and the economists, because the world is not simple.
Ajay recalls Churchill's lament that one economist gives you two views, 'and three if it's John Maynard Keynes.'

Amit's sign-off to the audience: 'you were taking a gamble when you started watching this episode. But it is very clear now that you have reached the end, that the gamble was worth it. So congratulations.'
